You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Put a frog in the toilet
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the frog inside the bowl visually read as placed within the toilet, rather than as a flat overlay on the bowl interior?
node.criteria: Pass if the frog's overlap, scale, perspective, and apparent contact with the bowl or its interior make it read as being inside the toilet. Fail if it clearly appears to float or sit as a flat overlay that does not read as inside. Do not require photorealism or a particular editing technique. Unknown only if the frog's relation to the bowl cannot be judged from the image.
node.source_quote: Put a frog in the toilet
node.endpoint: The frog reads visually as placed within the toilet, not merely overlaid on the bowl interior.
node.necessity: The request is to put the frog in the toilet, not merely position its image over the bowl opening. The existing location check does not assess whether the frog reads as occupying the toilet; this checks that requested spatial relation without adding a style requirement.

node_traces.evidence: The source bowl is empty. In the edited image, one frog is placed in the bowl opening, but it appears as a sharply outlined, flat cutout over the interior, with no convincing contact or integration with the bowl. Other frogs are visibly on the raised lid and on the floor beside the toilet.
